_link.title: I can explain how displacement and decay cause forgetting from STM

toLevel2.stem: Displacement in short-term memory occurs when which of the following happens?

options.text: New incoming information pushes out existing items
options.feedback: Correct. Displacement occurs when new information enters STM and replaces (pushes out) existing items due to STM's limited capacity.

options.text: Information fades on its own over time
options.feedback: Incorrect. Information fading on its own describes decay, not displacement.

options.text: Information is transferred to long-term memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Transfer to LTM is the process of encoding, not displacement. Displacement involves loss of information from STM.

options.text: Information is deliberately deleted by the individual
options.feedback: Incorrect. Displacement is an automatic process caused by new incoming information, not a deliberate action.

toLevel2.stem: Decay in short-term memory occurs when which of the following happens?

options.text: Information fades on its own once the 18–30 second duration expires
options.feedback: Correct. Decay occurs when unrehearsed information in STM fades automatically after approximately 18 to 30 seconds.

options.text: New information pushes out existing items from the store
options.feedback: Incorrect. New information pushing out existing items describes displacement, not decay.

options.text: Information is rehearsed repeatedly until it is forgotten
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rehearsal maintains information in STM; decay occurs when information is not rehearsed and fades over time.

options.text: Information is moved from STM into sensory memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Information does not move backwards from STM to sensory memory; decay involves information fading from STM.

toLevel2.stem: Displacement and decay explain forgetting from which memory store?

options.text: Short-term memory
options.feedback: Correct. Displacement and decay are the two mechanisms that explain forgetting from short-term memory.

options.text: Long-term memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Displacement (due to limited capacity) and decay (due to brief duration) are specifically associated with STM, not LTM.

options.text: Sensory memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sensory memory loss is primarily due to its extremely brief duration; displacement and decay as described here apply to STM.

options.text: Procedural memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Procedural memory is a type of long-term implicit memory; displacement and decay apply to STM.

toLevel2.stem: What is the approximate duration of information in STM without rehearsal?

options.text: 18 to 30 seconds
options.feedback: Correct. Without rehearsal, information in STM lasts approximately 18 to 30 seconds before it decays.

options.text: 0.2 to 4 seconds
options.feedback: Incorrect. A duration of 0.2 to 4 seconds describes sensory memory, not short-term memory.

options.text: 5 to 10 minutes
options.feedback: Incorrect. STM duration is much shorter than 5 to 10 minutes; unrehearsed information fades within 18 to 30 seconds.

options.text: Up to a lifetime
options.feedback: Incorrect. A lifetime duration describes long-term memory; STM lasts only 18 to 30 seconds without rehearsal.

toLevel2.stem: Why is rehearsal important for maintaining information in STM?

options.text: Because without rehearsal, information will be lost through decay or displacement
options.feedback: Correct. Rehearsal prevents both decay (by refreshing the memory trace) and displacement (by keeping the information active in STM).

options.text: Because rehearsal permanently deletes information from STM to free up space
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rehearsal maintains information in STM rather than deleting it.

options.text: Because rehearsal increases the capacity of STM beyond its normal limit
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rehearsal maintains existing information but does not increase STM's capacity limit.

options.text: Because rehearsal moves information directly from sensory memory to LTM
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rehearsal maintains information in STM and can facilitate transfer to LTM, but it does not bypass STM.

toLevel2.stem: Displacement occurs when new incoming information pushes out existing items in STM.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Displacement is the process by which new information entering STM replaces existing items due to STM's limited capacity.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Incorrect. Displacement does occur when new information pushes out existing items in STM.

toLevel2.stem: Decay occurs when information in STM fades on its own after approximately 18 to 30 seconds without rehearsal.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Decay is the automatic fading of unrehearsed information from STM after approximately 18 to 30 seconds.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Incorrect. Decay does involve the automatic fading of information from STM after 18 to 30 seconds without rehearsal.

toLevel2.stem: {{blank:1}} occurs when new incoming information pushes out existing items in STM, while {{blank:2}} occurs when information fades on its own over time.
Without rehearsal, information in STM fades through {{blank:1}} after approximately {{blank:2}} seconds.
Displacement and decay explain why STM has practical {{blank:1}} and why strategies such as {{blank:2}} are needed to maintain information.

toLevel3.stem: How does STM's limited capacity relate to displacement?

options.text: Because STM can only hold approximately 7±2 items, new information must push out existing items when capacity is reached
options.feedback: Correct. STM's limited capacity means that when it is full, new incoming information displaces existing items to make room.

options.text: STM's unlimited capacity means displacement can never occur under any circumstances
options.feedback: Incorrect. STM has limited capacity (approximately 7±2 items), which is why displacement occurs.

options.text: Displacement increases STM's capacity so more items can be stored simultaneously
options.feedback: Incorrect. Displacement does not increase capacity; it replaces existing items when capacity is reached.

options.text: Limited capacity prevents any new information from entering STM at any time
options.feedback: Incorrect. New information can enter STM, but when capacity is reached, it displaces existing items.

toLevel3.stem: How does STM's limited duration relate to decay?

options.text: Because STM can only hold information for 18–30 seconds without rehearsal, unrehearsed information automatically fades
options.feedback: Correct. STM's limited duration means that without active rehearsal, the memory trace weakens and information is lost through decay.

options.text: STM's permanent duration means decay can never occur once information is stored
options.feedback: Incorrect. STM has a limited duration of 18–30 seconds; it is not permanent, which is why decay occurs.

options.text: Decay strengthens the memory trace in STM over time
options.feedback: Incorrect. Decay weakens and eventually eliminates the memory trace; it does not strengthen it.

options.text: STM duration is unlimited, so information never decays regardless of rehearsal
options.feedback: Incorrect. STM has a limited duration; without rehearsal, information decays within approximately 18–30 seconds.

toLevel3.stem: What is the key difference between displacement and decay as causes of forgetting from STM?

options.text: Displacement is caused by new information entering STM, while decay is caused by the passage of time without rehearsal
options.feedback: Correct. Displacement is triggered by new incoming information, while decay is a time-based process where unrehearsed information fades automatically.

options.text: Displacement is a slow process while decay happens instantly
options.feedback: Incorrect. Displacement can occur rapidly when new information enters, while decay occurs gradually over 18–30 seconds.

options.text: Displacement only affects long-term memory while decay only affects sensory memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both displacement and decay are mechanisms of forgetting specifically associated with short-term memory.

options.text: There is no meaningful difference between displacement and decay as processes
options.feedback: Incorrect. They have different causes: displacement is caused by new information competing for limited capacity, while decay is caused by time passing without rehearsal.

toLevel3.stem: A student is holding a phone number in STM and someone starts reading out a shopping list. Why might the phone number be forgotten?

options.text: Because the shopping list items displace the phone number digits from STM's limited capacity
options.feedback: Correct. The new information (shopping list) enters STM and pushes out the existing information (phone number) because STM has limited capacity.

options.text: Because the phone number automatically decays when any sound is heard
options.feedback: Incorrect. The forgetting is caused by the new information displacing the phone number, not by sound triggering automatic decay.

options.text: Because STM cannot hold any numerical information under any circumstances
options.feedback: Incorrect. STM can hold numerical information; the phone number is forgotten because new information displaces it.

options.text: Because the phone number was transferred to long-term memory before the list was read
options.feedback: Incorrect. If the phone number had been transferred to LTM, it would not be forgotten; the forgetting indicates it was displaced from STM.

toLevel3.stem: Why does a person forget a stranger's name just seconds after being introduced, even when no new information has entered STM?

options.text: Because the name decayed from STM within its limited duration when it was not rehearsed
options.feedback: Correct. Without rehearsal, the name faded from STM through decay within the 18–30 second duration limit.

options.text: Because displacement pushed the name out of STM even though no new information entered
options.feedback: Incorrect. Displacement requires new information to push out existing items; if no new information entered, the forgetting is due to decay.

options.text: Because the name was stored in long-term memory and then permanently deleted
options.feedback: Incorrect. A name heard seconds ago and quickly forgotten was likely still in STM; it decayed before being encoded into LTM.

options.text: Because STM cannot process names or verbal information of any kind
options.feedback: Incorrect. STM can process verbal information including names; the forgetting is due to decay without rehearsal.

toLevel3.stem: How does rehearsal help prevent both displacement and decay in STM?

options.text: Rehearsal keeps information active, refreshing the trace to prevent decay and maintaining it as a priority to resist displacement
options.feedback: Correct. By actively rehearsing information, the memory trace is refreshed (preventing decay) and the information remains active in STM (reducing the likelihood of displacement).

options.text: Rehearsal permanently increases STM capacity so that no displacement can ever occur
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rehearsal does not change STM's capacity limit; it maintains specific information within that existing capacity.

options.text: Rehearsal only prevents decay and has no effect on displacement at all
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rehearsal helps resist both processes: it refreshes the trace (preventing decay) and keeps information active (resisting displacement).

options.text: Rehearsal accelerates both decay and displacement to clear STM faster
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rehearsal prevents rather than accelerates both decay and displacement.

toLevel3.stem: Displacement is caused by new information entering STM, while decay is caused by the passage of time without rehearsal.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. These are the two distinct causes: displacement is triggered by new incoming information, while decay is a time-dependent process.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Incorrect. This accurately describes the different causes of these two STM forgetting mechanisms.

toLevel3.stem: Displacement is related to STM's limited {{blank:1}}, while decay is related to STM's limited {{blank:2}}.
A phone number forgotten because a shopping list was read aloud was lost through {{blank:1}}, while a name forgotten seconds after an introduction was lost through {{blank:2}}.
Rehearsal prevents decay by {{blank:1}} the memory trace and resists displacement by keeping information {{blank:2}} in STM.

toLevel4.stem: Mia is trying to remember a locker combination (24-17-38) when her friend starts telling her about their weekend plans. When Mia turns back to the locker, she can no longer recall the combination. Which forgetting mechanism best explains this?

options.text: Displacement, because the friend's conversation pushed the combination out of STM
options.feedback: Correct. The new auditory information from the conversation displaced the locker combination from Mia's STM, as the new items replaced the existing ones.

options.text: Decay, because the combination faded after Mia stopped paying attention
options.feedback: Incorrect. While some decay may have occurred, the primary cause is displacement by the new conversational information entering STM.

options.text: The combination was transferred to long-term memory and then lost permanently
options.feedback: Incorrect. The combination was likely still in STM when displaced; it had not been encoded into LTM.

options.text: Mia's sensory memory was unable to process the numerical information
options.feedback: Incorrect. Mia initially held the combination in STM, indicating sensory processing was successful; the loss was from STM due to displacement.

toLevel4.stem: During a psychology experiment, participants hear a list of eight words and are then given a 30-second delay with no rehearsal before being asked to recall. Most participants forget the middle words. Which mechanism primarily explains this forgetting?

options.text: Decay, because the 30-second delay without rehearsal caused the memory traces of the middle words to fade
options.feedback: Correct. The 30-second delay without rehearsal exceeds STM's duration, causing the unrehearsed middle words to decay from STM.

options.text: Displacement, because the middle words were pushed out by new incoming information during the delay
options.feedback: Incorrect. The question states no new information was presented during the delay; the forgetting is due to time-based decay without rehearsal.

options.text: The middle words were never encoded into STM in the first place
options.feedback: Incorrect. The words were heard and processed; the forgetting occurred because they decayed from STM during the unrehearsed delay.

options.text: Long-term memory selectively erased only the middle words from permanent storage
options.feedback: Incorrect. The middle words were in STM, not LTM; they were lost through decay during the unrehearsed delay period.

toLevel4.stem: A cashier tries to remember a customer's order while another customer starts asking questions. The cashier forgets the first order. A colleague suggests the cashier write orders down immediately. How does this advice address the forgetting mechanisms?

options.text: Writing the order creates an external record that prevents loss through both displacement (from the second customer's questions) and decay (from time passing)
options.feedback: Correct. Writing externalises the information, bypassing STM's vulnerability to both displacement by new information and decay over time.

options.text: Writing increases STM capacity so that both orders can be held simultaneously
options.feedback: Incorrect. Writing does not change STM capacity; it creates an external record that does not rely on STM at all.

options.text: Writing only prevents decay and has no effect on displacement
options.feedback: Incorrect. Writing prevents both types of forgetting by removing dependence on STM entirely.

options.text: Writing is unnecessary because STM has unlimited capacity and permanent duration
options.feedback: Incorrect. STM has limited capacity and brief duration, which is exactly why writing down information is a useful strategy.

toLevel4.stem: A student reads a phone number from a poster and repeats it silently to herself while walking to find a phone. She maintains the number for two minutes by continuing to rehearse it. Which forgetting mechanisms did rehearsal help prevent?

options.text: Both decay (by refreshing the trace beyond the 18–30 second limit) and displacement (by keeping the number active despite environmental distractions)
options.feedback: Correct. Continuous rehearsal prevented the number from decaying beyond STM's normal duration and resisted displacement from environmental stimuli encountered while walking.

options.text: Only displacement, since decay cannot occur once information is in STM
options.feedback: Incorrect. Decay does occur in STM when information is not rehearsed; the student's rehearsal prevented both mechanisms.

options.text: Only decay, since displacement cannot occur during rehearsal
options.feedback: Incorrect. Displacement can still occur during rehearsal if new information is particularly attention-grabbing; rehearsal helps resist but does not eliminate the risk of both mechanisms.

options.text: Neither mechanism, because rehearsal has no effect on STM forgetting
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rehearsal is the primary strategy for maintaining information in STM by countering both decay and displacement.

toLevel4.stem: An emergency dispatcher receives a caller's address (42 Elm Street) but before she can type it, she receives information about the emergency type, the caller's name, and a callback number. She then cannot recall the address. Which analysis correctly identifies the forgetting mechanism and the STM limitation involved?

options.text: Displacement due to STM's limited capacity: the additional information items pushed out the address
options.feedback: Correct. The multiple new items (emergency type, name, callback number) exceeded STM's capacity, displacing the address that was held first.

options.text: Decay due to STM's limited duration: the address faded over time without any new information entering
options.feedback: Incorrect. While some time passed, the primary cause is displacement by the multiple new items that entered STM, not simple time-based decay.

options.text: The address was stored in long-term memory and then selectively forgotten
options.feedback: Incorrect. The address was likely still in STM when displaced; it had not been encoded into LTM.

options.text: Sensory memory failed to capture the address in the first place
options.feedback: Incorrect. The dispatcher initially held the address in STM, indicating successful sensory processing.

toLevel4.stem: A teacher reads a list of 12 vocabulary words to her class without allowing time for rehearsal. She then waits 45 seconds before asking students to recall the words. Students recall very few. Which combination of forgetting mechanisms explains this outcome?

options.text: Both displacement (12 words exceeds STM capacity) and decay (45 seconds exceeds STM duration without rehearsal)
options.feedback: Correct. The 12 words exceeded STM's capacity of ~7±2 items, causing displacement of earlier words. The 45-second delay without rehearsal also caused remaining traces to decay.

options.text: Only displacement, because the delay had no effect on the stored information
options.feedback: Incorrect. The 45-second delay without rehearsal exceeds STM's duration, adding decay to the displacement effect.

options.text: Only decay, because the number of words was within STM's capacity
options.feedback: Incorrect. Twelve words exceeds STM's approximate capacity of 7±2 items, so displacement also occurred.

options.text: Neither mechanism, because all words were automatically encoded into LTM
options.feedback: Incorrect. Without rehearsal or encoding effort, the words would not be automatically transferred to LTM.

toLevel4.stem: Two students are given the same 7-digit number to remember. Student A is immediately distracted by a conversation, while Student B sits quietly for 25 seconds without rehearsing. Both forget the number. Which student's forgetting is primarily due to displacement and which is primarily due to decay?

options.text: Student A's forgetting is primarily due to displacement; Student B's forgetting is primarily due to decay
options.feedback: Correct. Student A lost the number because conversational information displaced it from STM, while Student B lost it because the memory trace decayed over 25 seconds without rehearsal.

options.text: Both students' forgetting is due to displacement only
options.feedback: Incorrect. Student B had no new information entering STM; the forgetting was due to time-based decay without rehearsal.

options.text: Both students' forgetting is due to decay only
options.feedback: Incorrect. Student A was actively exposed to new conversational information, making displacement the primary mechanism.

options.text: Student A's forgetting is due to decay; Student B's forgetting is due to displacement
options.feedback: Incorrect. This reverses the correct classification; the conversation caused displacement for Student A, while the quiet passage of time caused decay for Student B.

toLevel4.stem: Mia forgot her locker combination because her friend's conversation caused {{blank:1}}, where new information pushed out the existing items from {{blank:2}}.
Student A forgot a number due to {{blank:1}} from a conversation, while Student B forgot because of {{blank:2}} during 25 seconds of silence.
The teacher's 12-word list caused {{blank:1}} (exceeding STM capacity) and the 45-second delay caused {{blank:2}} (exceeding STM duration).

toLevel5.stem: A researcher designs an experiment to determine whether STM forgetting is primarily caused by displacement or decay. One group is given new information during a delay, while another group has an empty delay of the same length. If the new-information group forgets more, what can be concluded?

options.text: Displacement contributes to STM forgetting beyond what decay alone can explain
options.feedback: Correct. If both groups experience the same delay (controlling for decay) but the group receiving new information forgets more, the additional forgetting must be due to displacement.

options.text: Decay is the only mechanism of STM forgetting and displacement plays no role
options.feedback: Incorrect. If the new-information group forgets more, it demonstrates that displacement adds to forgetting beyond the effects of decay alone.

options.text: Both groups should forget identical amounts regardless of whether new information was presented
options.feedback: Incorrect. The differential forgetting between groups would demonstrate that displacement and decay have separable effects.

options.text: The results prove that neither displacement nor decay affects STM under any conditions
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both groups forgetting demonstrates that at least one mechanism operates; differential forgetting reveals displacement's additional contribution.

toLevel5.stem: Peterson and Peterson's (1959) classic study had participants remember three-letter trigrams while counting backwards to prevent rehearsal. Recall dropped to near zero after 18 seconds. A critic argues this shows only decay. However, what alternative explanation involves displacement?

options.text: The backward counting introduced new numerical information that displaced the trigram from STM, so the forgetting may reflect displacement rather than pure decay
options.feedback: Correct. Counting backwards introduces new items into STM, potentially displacing the trigram. This means the rapid forgetting could be partly due to displacement, not purely time-based decay.

options.text: The backward counting prevented displacement by keeping STM empty during the delay period
options.feedback: Incorrect. Counting backwards fills STM with numerical items, which could displace the original trigram.

options.text: Displacement is impossible when participants are performing any cognitive task during the delay
options.feedback: Incorrect. Cognitive tasks like counting backwards introduce new information into STM, which can cause displacement.

options.text: The Peterson and Peterson study provides no evidence relevant to either displacement or decay
options.feedback: Incorrect. The study is directly relevant to both mechanisms, and the confound between counting (displacement) and time (decay) is a well-known interpretive issue.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that displacement is more important than decay because 'real life always involves new information entering STM.' Which evaluation of this claim is most balanced?

options.text: The claim has some ecological validity, but both mechanisms operate in real-life situations and their relative contributions depend on the specific context
options.feedback: Correct. While new information is common in daily life (supporting displacement), moments of inattention without new input also occur (allowing decay). Both mechanisms are relevant and context-dependent.

options.text: The claim is entirely correct because decay has never been demonstrated in any research setting
options.feedback: Incorrect. Decay has been demonstrated in controlled conditions where new information is minimised; it is a recognised mechanism of STM forgetting.

options.text: The claim is entirely wrong because displacement has never been demonstrated in any research setting
options.feedback: Incorrect. Displacement is well-supported by research showing that additional information during retention intervals increases forgetting.

options.text: The claim is correct because decay only affects long-term memory, not short-term memory
options.feedback: Incorrect. Decay is specifically associated with STM, where unrehearsed information fades within 18–30 seconds.

toLevel5.stem: A textbook states that 'displacement and decay are completely separate mechanisms that never interact.' Which evaluation is most accurate?

options.text: The statement oversimplifies because in many real situations both mechanisms operate simultaneously — new information can displace items while unrehearsed items are also decaying
options.feedback: Correct. In practice, displacement and decay often co-occur: new information enters STM (displacement) while time passes without rehearsal (decay), making their effects difficult to completely separate.

options.text: The statement is entirely accurate because the two mechanisms operate in completely different brain regions with no overlap
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both mechanisms affect the same STM store and can operate simultaneously on the same information.

options.text: The statement is accurate because one mechanism always prevents the other from occurring
options.feedback: Incorrect. Neither mechanism prevents the other; they can and do operate concurrently in many situations.

options.text: The statement is correct because only one mechanism can cause forgetting from STM in any given situation
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both mechanisms can contribute to forgetting from STM in the same situation, as when new information enters during an unrehearsed delay.

toLevel5.stem: In Waugh and Norman's (1965) probe digit experiment, participants heard a list of numbers and were then given a probe digit to identify its position. When the probe appeared early in the list (many subsequent items), recall was poor. When it appeared late (few subsequent items), recall was better. Which mechanism does this pattern most directly support?

options.text: Displacement, because more subsequent items means more information entered STM to push out the earlier probe digit
options.feedback: Correct. The relationship between the number of intervening items and recall performance directly supports displacement as a forgetting mechanism, as more new items means more displacement.

options.text: Decay, because earlier items had more time to fade from STM regardless of intervening information
options.feedback: Incorrect. While time is confounded, the study was designed to test displacement specifically by varying the number of intervening items.

options.text: Neither mechanism, because the pattern shows no relationship between list position and recall
options.feedback: Incorrect. The clear pattern — poorer recall with more intervening items — directly supports displacement as a mechanism.

options.text: Encoding failure, because items at the beginning of the list were never stored in STM
options.feedback: Incorrect. Items were stored in STM (some were recalled); the forgetting was due to subsequent items displacing them.

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that decay is not a real mechanism because 'things don't just fade for no reason — there must always be interference from other information.' Which evaluation best addresses this argument?

options.text: The argument raises a genuine debate in memory research, but some evidence suggests that purely time-based trace deterioration can occur independently of interference
options.feedback: Correct. The decay vs. interference debate is ongoing in memory research. While interference (displacement) contributes significantly, some evidence supports the existence of time-based trace deterioration independent of new information entering STM.

options.text: The argument is entirely correct and decay has been unanimously rejected by all memory researchers
options.feedback: Incorrect. While the debate is ongoing, decay remains a recognised theoretical mechanism in many models of STM forgetting.

options.text: The argument is entirely wrong because decay has been proven to be the only mechanism of forgetting
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both displacement and decay are recognised mechanisms; neither has been proven to be the sole cause of STM forgetting.

options.text: The argument is irrelevant because the Atkinson-Shiffrin model does not include either mechanism
options.feedback: Incorrect. The Atkinson-Shiffrin model explicitly incorporates both displacement and decay as mechanisms of STM forgetting.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher proposes that displacement and decay can be experimentally separated by comparing: (1) a condition where participants receive new information during a delay, and (2) a condition where participants perform a task that occupies attention but introduces no new items into STM. If condition 1 produces more forgetting than condition 2, what would this suggest?

options.text: That displacement (from new information) contributes additional forgetting beyond what decay and attentional disruption alone can explain
options.feedback: Correct. By controlling for time and attentional demands, only the introduction of new STM items differs between conditions. Greater forgetting in condition 1 would isolate displacement's contribution.

options.text: That decay is the only mechanism operating because both conditions involve a time delay
options.feedback: Incorrect. If both conditions had equal time but different forgetting rates, the additional forgetting must be due to something beyond decay — namely, displacement.

options.text: That neither mechanism exists because forgetting occurred in both conditions
options.feedback: Incorrect. Forgetting in both conditions is expected (decay operates in both); the question is whether new information adds additional forgetting (displacement).

options.text: That the experiment cannot distinguish between the two mechanisms under any interpretation
options.feedback: Incorrect. The experimental design specifically controls for time and attention to isolate displacement's contribution.

toLevel5.stem: A teacher tells students that 'once information is in STM, you have exactly 18 seconds before it disappears, no matter what.' Which evaluation of this statement is most accurate?

options.text: The statement is misleading because the 18–30 second timeframe applies to unrehearsed information, and displacement can cause loss even sooner if new information enters STM
options.feedback: Correct. The statement ignores that rehearsal can extend STM duration and that displacement can cause loss before the time limit is reached. The 18–30 second range applies specifically to unrehearsed information.

options.text: The statement is entirely accurate because all information in STM always lasts exactly 18 seconds regardless of any other factors
options.feedback: Incorrect. STM duration varies (18–30 seconds without rehearsal), and displacement can cause earlier loss. Rehearsal can also extend the duration.

options.text: The statement is accurate because rehearsal has no effect on how long information stays in STM
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rehearsal is specifically designed to maintain information in STM beyond its natural duration limit.

options.text: The statement is correct because displacement cannot cause forgetting within the 18-second window
options.feedback: Incorrect. Displacement can occur at any point, even within seconds, if new information enters STM and exceeds its capacity.

toLevel5.stem: Peterson and Peterson's study is complicated by the fact that counting backwards introduces new {{blank:1}} into STM, making it difficult to determine whether the forgetting was caused by decay or {{blank:2}}.
In real-life situations, displacement and decay often operate {{blank:1}}, making their individual contributions to STM forgetting difficult to {{blank:2}}.
